rule.statement: From each archived NASA ephemeris only the first orbit is used: its one-orbit mean semi-major axis. Between consecutive files the change, minus the earlier file's own drag decay, is a burn; |delta-v| >= 0.2 m/s in a gap of at most 7 days is a detection. Fixed in code before the announcements were collected.

burns.note: delta-v from the report's SAMS interval average
post says 9:25 a.m., read as Eastern Daylight Time (UTC-4); 10 min 23 s burn; no delta-v given
magnitude of the report's SAMS estimate (its sign is the sensor axis)

ISS Daily Summary Report for 2022-10-17: 'Today, the ISS successfully performed a reboost using the Progress 81P thrusters.' Date only (time set to noon, so up to 12 h off). NASA's header table had listed it for 2022-10-20. Looked up after the detector flagged this gap.
'Thruster firing occurred at 7:42 AM CST' (UTC-6), 10 min 21 s, delta-v 1.0 m/s. NASA's header table had listed a reboost for 2022-12-24 instead. Looked up after the detector flagged this gap.

Roscosmos via Interfax: engines on at '3:42 p.m. Moscow time' (UTC+3), 375.8 s, 0.7 m/s. NASA's blog also reported a little over six minutes of Progress 83 thrusters on March 6 (as quoted by news outlets; the post itself was not retrieved). Looked up after the detector flagged this gap.
Roscosmos via Interfax: engines on at '2:54 p.m. Moscow time' (UTC+3), 155 s, 0.3 m/s, mean altitude up 500 m (preliminary). Looked up after the detector flagged this gap.
text says '233/14:35' but its date is 2023-08-11 (day 223) and its figure axis reads 223: day 223 used

NASA: Zvezda engines 'fired for 21.5 seconds beginning at 11 a.m. EDT' (UTC-4); no delta-v. Roscosmos via Interfax (https://www.interfax.com/newsroom/top-stories/93923/): the maneuver 'tentatively lowered the orbit of the ISS by 500 meters'. Looked up after the detector flagged this gap.

aborted_attempts.note: 10:20 a.m. Central (UTC-5); 5 s of a planned 5 min 1 s burn, so about 1/60 of the planned 0.3 m/s: below any detector, not scored as a burn

current_file.note: NASA's header table and the forecast itself carry planned burns, so a 'prediction' read from them would repeat NASA's plan, not test the detector. Only a detection between two published files (a burn that already happened) is registered, and it states whether NASA had listed it.
